mappings.note: Requires the usual occupation of each landform - tourism, mining, terrace farming, herding - and spotting the mismatch, so LO-47 with LO-32 for the landforms themselves. Not LO-27, no plant or animal life is at issue.
Statement set on snow cover, plateau height and plain fertility - all properties of the landforms LO-32 names. Not LO-47, since no occupation is judged.

Why the earliest civilisations grew on river plains is the beginning-of-agriculture-and-first-cities development that LO-38 names outright; LO-32 carries the river and plain. Not LO-47, which is about present-day rural and urban occupations.
Palai as the parched tinai of Sangam poetry - content described in an ancient literary work, so LO-36 with the other tinai items rather than LO-32's real deserts.
Defines a lichen, an organism of the high-altitude biosphere. Not LO-32: the item is about living things, not about the landform they cling to.
Matches peaks to their ranges and regions across continents (Mont Blanc in the Alps against African and South Indian distractors) - a world-map item, hence LO-30.
Identifies a plateau from its flat top, steep sides and waterfalls; landform recognition under LO-32, the same reading as the other plateau-description items.

Flash floods, avalanches, cold and hard transport as the burdens of mountain life: the earth as a human habitat, which only the goal states. LO-32 would describe the mountain, not the difficulty of living on it, and this is mapped like the landslide item.
Defines 'terrain' as land seen through its physical features - the vocabulary underpinning LO-32's mountains, plateaus and plains.
One-line recall that a natural surface feature is a landform; the short-answer twin of the earlier definition item.
Names mountains, plateaus and plains - literally the list LO-32 enumerates.
Altitude as height above sea level; the measure separating the landforms of LO-32. Again not LO-31, which concerns latitude and longitude.
Hills as lower, round-topped highlands - a distinction inside LO-32's landform vocabulary, the recall form of the mountain-versus-hill item.
Snow as the solid form of precipitation at cold heights - water moving between the earth's zones, which is LO-27. Not LO-32, no landform is named.
Names a mountain range on the continent of Asia, so the demand is world-map placement. The India-specific Himalayan items are mapped to LO-32.
Everest as the world's highest peak - a world-map superlative, hence LO-30 rather than the Indian-features outcome.

About 40 crore people living in the Ganga plain is a statement about where humans are concentrated on the earth's surface, which the goal CG-SST1 covers as habitat and distribution. LO-32 would only place the plain; the item is about the population it carries.
Names a crop of the Gangetic plain: the farming that this landform makes available (LO-47), on a named Indian plain (LO-32).
Confluence as the meeting of rivers - river vocabulary under LO-32, the recall twin of the earlier multiple-choice version.
Broad base, steep slopes, narrow summit: the defining shape of a mountain, a landform property under LO-32.
Why high peaks stay snow-capped - freezing temperatures at altitude, a consequence of the mountain's height. Not LO-27, because the item explains the snow's persistence, not water's role in life.
Young versus old mountains by age, height and peak shape; a comparison within LO-32's mountain category.
Describes montane conifers in detail - plant life of a zone of the earth, so LO-27 with the other vegetation items rather than the landform outcome.
Why herding beats farming on rugged slopes - the terrain deciding which occupation is available, which is exactly what LO-47 asks pupils to describe.
Plateaus as mineral stores (LO-32) and therefore mining sites (LO-47). The assertion-reason version of this item was mapped the same way, since both halves are genuinely in the question.
How lava-plateau soil differs from other plateau soil - a comparison of landform properties, so LO-32 alone; the farming consequence is only a trailing remark.
What makes floodplains good for agriculture; the question is pointed at the farming (LO-47), resting on the sediment that builds the plain (LO-32).
Desert characteristics: a dry expanse with little precipitation (LO-32 names deserts) and flora and fauna adapted to it (LO-27). Both halves are asked for.
Precipitation and its forms - rain, snow and hail moving water between the earth's zones, which is LO-27's subject.
Erosion wearing mountains down over time; a process shaping the landforms of LO-32, and the mechanism behind the young-versus-old contrast.
Compares the altitude of plains with that of mountains - two of LO-32's categories set against each other by height.

The significance of river sediment in the plains; asked from the landform side (LO-32), with the farming and dense settlement it permits as the consequence (LO-47). The floodplain-agriculture item takes the same pair in the reverse order because it is asked from the farming side.

Hot versus cold deserts with the Sahara and the Gobi as examples. LO-32 is the only outcome naming deserts as a landform type; the foreign examples are illustrations of the type, not a world-map placement task, so LO-30 would be wrong.
The chapter's summative question: how the three landforms form (LO-32) and how each shapes farming, herding, mining and tourism (LO-47). Both are explicitly demanded by the stem.
Himalayas against the Aravallis on height, peak shape and stability - two named Indian ranges compared as landforms, so LO-32 and not the world-map outcome.
Plateaus as mineral stores and as waterfall sites, with named examples (LO-32), tied to mining and hydro-power (LO-47). Longer than the short-answer version but the same two outcomes.
